imo-2014-01.title: A strictly decreasing auxiliary sequence
imo-2014-01.body:
For $n\ge1$ let
$$d_n=(a_0+a_1+\cdots+a_n)-na_n .$$
- The left inequality $a_n<\frac{a_0+\cdots+a_n}{n}$ is equivalent to $d_n>0$.
- The right inequality $a_0+\cdots+a_n\le na_{n+1}$ is equivalent to $a_0+\cdots+a_{n+1}\le(n+1)a_{n+1}$, i.e. to $d_{n+1}\le0$.

So we need a unique $n\ge1$ with $d_n>0\ge d_{n+1}$.

Now $d_1=a_0>0$, and
$$d_{n+1}-d_n=a_{n+1}-(n+1)a_{n+1}+na_n=n(a_n-a_{n+1})<0,$$
so $(d_n)$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of integers; it decreases by at least $1$ at each step and therefore eventually becomes $\le0$. Let $n$ be the largest index with $d_n>0$ (it exists because $d_1>0$ and $d_m\le 0$ for large $m$). Then $d_n>0\ge d_{n+1}$. For any other index $m$: if $m<n$ then $d_{m+1}\ge d_n>0$, and if $m>n$ then $d_m\le d_{n+1}\le0$; either way $m$ fails. Hence $n$ is unique. ∎

imo-2014-02.title: An empty square when $n>\ell^2$, a construction when $n\le\ell^2$
imo-2014-02.body:
For a positive integer $\ell$ we show: **(i)** if $n>\ell^2$, every peaceful configuration has an empty $\ell\times\ell$ square; **(ii)** if $n\le\ell^2$, some peaceful configuration has none. Then the greatest $k$ is the largest $\ell$ with $\ell^2<n$, i.e. $k=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$. (Note $k\ge1$ as $n\ge2$.)

**(i)** Let $n>\ell^2$. Some row $R$ has its rook in the leftmost column. Choose $\ell$ consecutive rows including $R$; their union $U$ contains exactly $\ell$ rooks. Delete from $U$ its $n-\ell^2\ge1$ leftmost columns; this removes at least the rook of $R$. The remaining $\ell\times\ell^2$ rectangle contains at most $\ell-1$ rooks and splits into $\ell$ disjoint $\ell\times\ell$ squares, so one of them is empty.

**(ii)** *First $n=\ell^2$.* Number rows and columns $0,1,\dots,\ell^2-1$ and put rooks on the squares (row, column) $=(i\ell+j,\ j\ell+i)$ for $0\le i,j\le\ell-1$. Each number in $[0,\ell^2-1]$ has a unique form $i\ell+j$, so this is peaceful. Take any $\ell\times\ell$ square; its rows are $\ell$ consecutive rows, the lowest being $p\ell+q$ ($0\le p,q\le\ell-1$, $p\ell+q\le\ell^2-\ell$). The rooks in these rows are in the columns
$$p+1,\ \ell+p+1,\ \dots,\ (q-1)\ell+p+1,\qquad q\ell+p,\ (q+1)\ell+p,\ \dots,\ (\ell-1)\ell+p$$
(rows $p\ell+q,\dots,p\ell+\ell-1$ give the second list and rows $(p+1)\ell,\dots,(p+1)\ell+q-1$ the first). In increasing order, the first of these is at most $\ell-1$ (if $q\ge1$ then $p\le\ell-2$; if $q=0$ it is $p$), the last is at least $(\ell-1)\ell$, and consecutive ones differ by at most $\ell$. The square's columns form a block of $\ell$ consecutive columns $c,\dots,c+\ell-1$ with $0\le c\le\ell^2-\ell$, so it contains one of these columns, and the rook there lies in the square.

*Now $n<\ell^2$.* Take the configuration above and delete the bottom $\ell^2-n$ rows and the rightmost $\ell^2-n$ columns. Every $\ell\times\ell$ square of the remaining $n\times n$ board still contains a rook, but some rows and columns may have lost their rook. The number of empty rows equals the number of empty columns (each remaining rook occupies one row and one column); pair them up and add a rook at each crossing of a paired empty row and column. The configuration is peaceful and still has no empty $\ell\times\ell$ square.

**Answer:** $k=\lfloor\sqrt{n-1}\rfloor$. ∎

imo-2014-03.title: Circumcentres on the sides, then a ratio (official solution, reworded)
imo-2014-03.body:
**Step 1: the circumcentre $K$ of $SHC$ lies on $AB$.** Let the line through $C$ perpendicular to $SC$ meet line $AB$ at $Q$. In the right triangle $SCQ$,
$$\angle SQC=90^\circ-\angle QSC=90^\circ-\angle BSC=180^\circ-\angle SHC,$$
using the hypothesis $\angle SHC=90^\circ+\angle BSC$. So $S,H,C,Q$ are concyclic, and since $\angle SCQ=90^\circ$, $SQ$ is a diameter of this circle; its centre $K$ lies on $SQ$, i.e. on line $AB$. Similarly the circumcentre $L$ of $THC$ lies on line $AD$.

**Step 2: reduction.** The centre of the circle $TSH$ lies on the perpendicular bisectors of $HS$ and $HT$. The circle is tangent to $BD$ at $H$ if and only if its centre lies on the line through $H$ perpendicular to $BD$, which is line $AH$. Since $KS=KH$ with $S$ on line $KA$, the perpendicular bisector of $HS$ is the bisector of $\angle AKH$; it meets $AH$ at the point $P$ with $\frac{AP}{PH}=\frac{AK}{KH}$. Likewise the perpendicular bisector of $HT$ meets $AH$ at the point $P'$ with $\frac{AP'}{P'H}=\frac{AL}{LH}$. So it suffices to prove
$$\frac{AK}{KH}=\frac{AL}{LH}. \tag{1}$$

**Step 3: proof of (1).** As $KH=KC$ and $LH=LC$, the line $KL$ is the perpendicular bisector of $HC$; let it meet $HC$ at its midpoint $M$, so $CM\perp KL$. The circumcircle of $ABCD$ has diameter $AC$ (right angles at $B,D$); its centre $O$ is the midpoint of $AC$. In triangle $CAH$, $OM\parallel AH$, so $OM\perp BD$; since $OB=OD$, $M$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$: $BM=DM$.

Since $\angle KBC=90^\circ$ and $\angle KMC=90^\circ$, the points $B,M$ lie on the circle with diameter $KC$; similarly $D,M$ lie on the circle with diameter $LC$. A chord of a circle equals the diameter times the sine of an inscribed angle on it, so
$$\sin\angle AKL=\sin\angle BKM=\frac{BM}{KC},\qquad \sin\angle ALK=\sin\angle DLM=\frac{DM}{LC}.$$
By the sine law in triangle $AKL$,
$$\frac{AK}{AL}=\frac{\sin\angle ALK}{\sin\angle AKL}=\frac{DM}{LC}\cdot\frac{KC}{BM}=\frac{KC}{LC}=\frac{KH}{LH},$$
which is (1). Hence the perpendicular bisectors of $HS$ and $HT$ meet on $AH$, the circumcentre of $TSH$ lies on the perpendicular to $BD$ at $H$, and $BD$ is tangent to the circle $TSH$ at $H$. ∎

imo-2014-04.title: Similar triangles and an angle sum
imo-2014-04.body:
Write $\angle A,\angle B,\angle C$ for the angles of the triangle.

**Two similarities.** Triangles $ABP$ and $CBA$ share the angle at $B$ and $\angle BAP=\angle BCA$, so $\triangle ABP\sim\triangle CBA$ (with $A\leftrightarrow C$, $B\leftrightarrow B$, $P\leftrightarrow A$). Hence
$$\frac{AB}{CB}=\frac{BP}{BA}=\frac{AP}{CA},\qquad \angle APB=\angle CAB=\angle A .$$
Similarly $\triangle ACQ\sim\triangle BCA$ (with $A\leftrightarrow B$, $C\leftrightarrow C$, $Q\leftrightarrow A$), so
$$\frac{AC}{BC}=\frac{CQ}{CA}=\frac{AQ}{BA},\qquad \angle AQC=\angle A .$$

**$AP=AQ$.** Both ratios give $AP=\frac{AB\cdot AC}{BC}=AQ$. Hence $PM=AP=AQ=QN$.

**A third similarity.** From the first similarity, $\frac{BP}{PM}=\frac{BP}{AP}=\frac{BA}{CA}$; from the second, $\frac{NQ}{QC}=\frac{AQ}{QC}=\frac{AB}{CA}$. So
$$\frac{BP}{PM}=\frac{NQ}{QC}.$$
Since $P$ is between $A$ and $M$ and between $B$ and $C$, the vertical angles give $\angle BPM=\angle APC=180^\circ-\angle A$; likewise $\angle NQC=\angle AQB=180^\circ-\angle A$. By SAS, $\triangle BPM\sim\triangle NQC$ (with $B\leftrightarrow N$, $P\leftrightarrow Q$, $M\leftrightarrow C$), hence
$$\angle PBM=\angle QNC .$$

**The intersection point.** The points $M$ and $N$ lie on the opposite side of $BC$ from $A$. In triangle $NQC$,
$$\angle MBC+\angle NCB=\angle QNC+\angle NCQ=180^\circ-\angle NQC=\angle A<180^\circ .$$
So the rays $BM$ and $CN$, which go into the same half-plane bounded by $BC$, meet at a point $X$ on the side of $BC$ opposite to $A$, and in triangle $BXC$
$$\angle BXC=180^\circ-(\angle XBC+\angle XCB)=180^\circ-\angle A .$$
Since $X$ and $A$ lie on opposite sides of $BC$ and $\angle BXC+\angle BAC=180^\circ$, the quadrilateral $ABXC$ is cyclic: $X$ lies on the circumcircle of $ABC$. ∎

imo-2014-05.title: Reduce, box the large coins, then add the small ones greedily
imo-2014-05.body:
We prove for every $k\ge1$: **any finite collection of total value at most $k-\frac12$ can be split into at most $k$ groups of value at most $1$.** The problem is the case $k=100$. We use induction on $k$ and, for fixed $k$, on the number of coins.

**Reduction 1.** If two coins $\frac1{2m}$ are present, replace them by one coin $\frac1m$ (same total, fewer coins). A valid split of the new collection gives a valid split of the old one: put both $\frac1{2m}$ coins into the group of the $\frac1m$ coin.

**Reduction 2.** If $2m+1$ coins $\frac1{2m+1}$ are present ($m\ge0$), they form a group of value exactly $1$. The rest has value at most $(k-1)-\frac12$; for $k=1$ this is impossible (total $\ge1>\frac12$), and for $k\ge2$ the rest splits into $k-1$ groups by induction.

So assume neither reduction applies: there is at most one coin of each even denomination $\frac1{2m}$ and at most $2m$ coins of each odd denomination $\frac1{2m+1}$; in particular no coin equals $1$.

**Boxes.** For $m=0,1,\dots,k-1$ put into box $B_m$ all coins $\frac1{2m+1}$ and $\frac1{2m+2}$. Its value is at most
$$\frac{2m}{2m+1}+\frac1{2m+2}<\frac{2m}{2m+1}+\frac1{2m+1}=1 .$$
The remaining coins all have value at most $\frac1{2k+1}$.

**Greedy step.** Put the remaining coins one by one into any box where the value stays at most $1$. Suppose some coin $c\le\frac1{2k+1}$ fits nowhere. Then each of the $k$ boxes already has value greater than $1-c\ge1-\frac1{2k+1}$, so the total value exceeds
$$k\left(1-\frac1{2k+1}\right)=k-\frac{k}{2k+1}>k-\frac12,$$
contradicting the hypothesis. So all coins are placed into the $k$ boxes, each of value at most $1$.

With $k=100$ and total at most $99+\frac12=100-\frac12$, at most $100$ groups suffice. ∎

imo-2014-06.title: A maximal blue set and a charging argument (official comment, reworded)
imo-2014-06.body:
Call a set of lines *admissible* if colouring exactly these lines blue leaves no finite region with an all-blue boundary. Subsets of admissible sets are admissible. Choose an admissible set $B$ that is maximal under inclusion, let $k=|B|$, and colour the other $n-k$ lines red. It suffices to show $n\le k^2$, because then $k\ge\sqrt n$ (and we may keep any $\lceil\sqrt n\,\rceil$ of the blue lines).

Call a point *blue* if it is the intersection of two blue lines (there are $\binom k2$ of them), and *red* if it is the intersection of a red line and a blue line.

**Assigning red lines to blue points.** Let $\ell$ be a red line. By maximality, $B\cup\{\ell\}$ is not admissible, so some finite region $A$ has all sides blue except those on $\ell$. A convex region has at most one side on a given line, so exactly one side of $A$, say $r'r$, lies on $\ell$. List the vertices of $A$ clockwise as $r',r,b_1,\dots,b_j$ ($j\ge1$ because $A$ has at least three sides). The side $rb_1$ lies on a blue line, so $r$ is a red point; and $b_1$ is the meeting point of two consecutive sides of $A$ other than $r'r$, both blue, so $b_1$ is a blue point. **Assign $\ell$ to the blue point $b_1$.** Note that $r$ lies on exactly two lines, $\ell$ and the blue line $rb_1$, and that the segment $b_1r$ contains no other intersection points (it is a side of $A$): $r$ is the first point after $b_1$ where some other line crosses that ray from $b_1$.

**Each blue point receives at most two red lines.** Suppose distinct red lines $\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3$ are assigned to the same blue point $b$, with regions $A_1,A_2,A_3$ and red points $r_1,r_2,r_3$ as above. Each $r_i$ is the first crossing point on one of the four rays from $b$ along the two blue lines through $b$; and the $r_i$ are distinct, since $r_i$ determines $\ell_i$ (the only red line through it). So $r_1,r_2,r_3$ are on three different rays. Two of these rays are opposite rays of one blue line $m$ through $b$, and the third lies on the other blue line; relabel so that $r_2,r_3\in m$ and $r_1$ lies on the other line.

Now look at the region $A_1$: clockwise it has the consecutive vertices $r_1$, $b$. The two sides of $A_1$ at $b$ lie along the two blue lines through $b$; one of them is $br_1$, so the other runs from $b$ along $m$, in one of its two directions, and ends at the first crossing point in that direction, which is $r_2$ or $r_3$, say $r_2$. So $r_2$ is a vertex of $A_1$ other than $r_1$ lying on a red line. But the only vertices of $A_1$ on red lines are $r_1$ and $r_1'$, so $r_2=r_1'$, and the side $r_1'r_1$ of $A_1$ lies on $\ell_1$; thus $\ell_1$ passes through $r_2$. The point $r_2$ lies only on the lines $m$ (blue) and $\ell_2$, so $\ell_1=\ell_2$, a contradiction.

**Counting.** Every red line is assigned to a blue point and each blue point receives at most two, so
$$n-k\le2\binom k2=k^2-k,$$
i.e. $n\le k^2$ and $k\ge\sqrt n$. This holds for every $n$, in particular for all sufficiently large $n$. ∎
